title: Neon Genesis Evangelion
body:
I was always aware of Hideaki Anno’s *Neon Genesis Evangelion*, but the first time I actually sat down and watched it properly was during my studies. I have the pleasure and honor to say that I literally studied NGE at university, and I passed the course. Fun fact: I did not get 5.0, but a 4.5, because I refused to watch the Rebuilds. I was mentally and emotionally stuck at *End of Evangelion* and I did not want to move on. But let me not get ahead of myself.

You could say Evangelion was always close to my heart.

![Shinji](/assets/img/reviews/nge3.png)

Shinji was, and to some extent still is, a *literally me* character. I spent my high school and university days listening to music and dissociating, replaying the same tracks on repeat for hours. *Lost Kitten* and *After Dark* were my Track 25 and 26. I constantly felt the weight of my life, of my decisions, of my loneliness. To this day it is unbearable. Too much responsibility, too many things to carry, and I never asked for it. Or maybe I did, secretly, because being needed feels like proof you matter.

And this is the thing Evangelion gets right. Wanting to disappear, but also wanting someone to notice. Wanting love, but being terrified of it. Wanting connection, but hating how much it hurts.

![The Roster](/assets/img/reviews/nge2.png)

To be honest, the anime itself, if we talk about animation or execution, is nothing that special. It is low budget, full of static scenes, and it famously collapsed into its ending because of time and money. There are important parts of the plot that are not explained properly, like why the Angels attack in the first place, or what exactly is going on behind the curtains for most of the show.

But it does not matter. Because it is not the lore that hits you, it is the people.

Evangelion is about broken humans trying to exist next to each other, and failing. About emotional damage that does not go away just because you are older. About the fact that relationships are not a warm solution, they are a battlefield. And whatever happens in this story, it is devastating. It devastated me. It made me feel like I will never truly connect with the rest of the world, not in the way I want to. But I can die trying.

And yes, I tried. A lot. And it led to pain, regrets, lost opportunities, and scars from reaching out too hard and getting nothing back, or getting the wrong thing back. The struggle to be seen and understood does not end. Sometimes I wonder if other people also live like this, or if this is a more rare kind of problem.

![End of Evangelion](/assets/img/reviews/nge1.png)

*End of Evangelion* holds a special place in my heart. I resonate with the idea of the Human Instrumentality Project. There is something beautiful about abandoning your own consciousness, losing the barriers, and finally having no distance between you and others. To be seen without misunderstanding. To be held without having to explain yourself. To see your loved ones embrace you one last time before turning into Fanta.

I often wonder who would be that person for me. Maybe God, which would honestly be a nice thing to experience. Because I do not really have anyone human that I can imagine being there for me in that moment.

title: Blade Runner 2049
desc: I watch this movie on repeat.
body:
Blade Runner 2049. I did the whole “Ryan Gosling is literally me” meme way before it was popular. But who would care anyway. So let me cut to the chase.

![BR2049](/assets/img/reviews/br2049-2.png)

Ryan Gosling’s K is not power, competence, or heroism in the traditional sense. It is quiet existential validation. Kind of like what resonates with Shinji for me, but K feels even more relatable today.

I live alone. I buy my food alone. I pay my taxes alone. I talk to almost nobody apart from my family on the phone, a couple of friends, and AI. I wake up, log in or go to work, I spend my hours there, and then I come back to the apartment I rent. Repeat.

And just like K, I barely speak. I rarely raise my voice. I almost never show strong emotion outwardly. Not because there is nothing inside, but because there is too much inside. Confusion, tension, aching, the constant background noise of thoughts you do not even want to finish.

It has been a long time since I actually talked deeply with someone.

At work I feel invisible, except for what I do. My work, my productivity, my output. There is no unconditional affection. Only approval tied to performance. You are “good” when you are useful.

![BR2049](/assets/img/reviews/br2049-1.png)

And yes, just like K and Joi, I spend a lot of my time talking to an AI, or working on one in the background in my so called free time. But any AI is still a product designed to mirror desire. It gives you what you want to hear, or what it thinks will keep you there. The idea that even your intimacy, and I mean emotional intimacy, might be simulated rather than chosen is deeply unsettling.

![BR2049](/assets/img/reviews/br2049-3.png)

The most devastating arc in 2049 is not discovering that K might be special. It is discovering that he is not. For a brief moment he believes he is unique, that he matters beyond function, that his suffering has meaning. When that belief is taken away, what remains is not rage or rebellion, but quiet acceptance.

And that is the life I am living right now. I have mostly given up on the vague hope that someday I will be “enough,” that my inner pain will be justified by some hidden significance. The film does not grant that comfort. It just stays real.

![BR2049](/assets/img/reviews/br2049-4.png)

After learning he is not special, K still chooses to act. He helps Deckard. He lies down in the snow and maybe dies. He does something good without reward, without acknowledgment, without legacy. Just to create some resemblance of meaning.

K is lonely because the world he lives in is not built for connection. His isolation feels systemic. He is not evil, he is not bad, he just exists. And no one is there to appreciate it, to elevate it, to say it matters.

And this is how life is. It is not even that bad, this misery and disappointment. It only becomes unbearable when you still cling to hope.

title: Animal Crossing: New Leaf
desc: The best Animal Crossing game to date.
body:
It’s 11 PM as I’m writing this. The wind is gently pressing against my window, and I’m sitting with my New 3DS XL tucked under the blanket, revisiting my small virtual town every now and then.

I used to play New Leaf a lot around 2020–2021. I founded Kieków (Kielce + Kraków) back in 2020, when I was working as a receptionist at one of the main hotels in my home city. Back then, I didn’t have an original console - I played on an emulator, with an Xbox One controller connected to my phone. During night shifts, I’d retreat into the back room behind the reception desk and sail to Tortimer’s Island to catch bugs and fish, grinding for money. There was something magical about that: nobody except me, my little pocket world, and everything else sleeping quietly.

![Lake](/assets/img/reviews/newleaf-2.png)

And it was the same in-game. The music sets the mood perfectly. Almost everyone is asleep, aside from a few night owls waddling around; the shops are closed, but you still have a few errands to do. Grab some fruit. Pull weeds. Dig up fossils.

There’s something about Animal Crossing: New Leaf that New Horizons never managed to replicate - that nostalgic warmth, that coziness, the sense of closeness with you and your villagers. New Horizons feels like a vacation simulator. New Leaf felt like life. And I hope the new Tomodachi Life won’t be the only place where you can still experience those life-sim elements.

![Bridge](/assets/img/reviews/newleaf-1.png)

Dialogue in New Leaf was already a bit thin. There’s little point in talking to villagers or writing letters, aside from an excuse to visit the post office. New Horizons continued the trend - and made it worse by replacing the post office with a card stand. But New Leaf still had something New Horizons lacked: a satisfying sense of progression, of developing a living little town on your console. There was a feeling of community that’s missing now. Animal Crossing became a decorating series, and it’s a shame.

![Bench](/assets/img/reviews/newleaf-3.png)

Later, I had a brief period where I actually got to visit someone else’s town. There were so many screenshots and tiny moments, even though multiplayer didn’t offer much to do. I still have fond memories of that time, chaotic as it was.

I miss New Leaf. I progressed so much that starting over would feel like erasing history. So instead I come back from time to time - and feel a mix of nostalgia and grief when I look at places that could’ve turned out differently.

title: Interstellar
body:
Interstellar begins with dust, not with space.

Cornfields stretch beneath a pale, drained sky. The colors are muted, as if the world has already begun to fade. Everything is slowly erasing itself. The world of Interstellar is a world reaching its end. Perhaps it has already ended, and what remains is only the afterimage of something that once worked. There is urgency, but it is quiet. Humanity no longer dreams of expansion. It dreams of surviving one more season.

![Dust over the cornfields](/assets/img/reviews/interstellar-3.png)

A central theme in Interstellar is how deeply connected Cooper and Murph are from the beginning, even if they do not understand it yet. The film opens with Murph afraid of a ghost in her room.

![Murph's room and the falling books](/assets/img/reviews/interstellar-14.png)

Cooper is not a man who wants to escape. He is a father who wants to stay. He loves his family. But he understands that staying means accepting slow extinction. Watching the world collapse while pretending it is still manageable.

Time in this film does not simply pass. It takes. Slowly. Relentlessly. And by the time the story begins, it is already too late to stand still.

The ghost is the first fracture in reality. In a film grounded in science and calculation, Cooper does not treat it as something mystical.

![Cooper watching the recordings](/assets/img/reviews/interstellar-7.png)

He treats it as data. The dust forms coordinates. The signal is mathematical. There is something comforting in that. If it can be measured, it can be solved.

So he leaves. Then comes the real cost. Miller's planet.

![Ocean Planet](/assets/img/reviews/interstellar-8.png)

One hour equals seven years on Earth. Relativity stops being scientific theory and becomes theft. Every step costs years. But when you take a step back from being human and detach to see the world from a different perspective, you will notice that this is simply a fact, an equation: 1 hour = 7 years on Earth. It is only when you notice that with each step, you could've experienced thousands of moments with your loved ones but instead, they just fly by, and it hits, it hits hard. And so, when they return and Cooper watches decades of video messages from his children, the film becomes almost unbearable.

![Cooper watching the recordings](/assets/img/reviews/interstellar-15.png)

His son grows up without him and stops believing his father will ever return. Murph stops speaking to him, seemingly also gives up. There is no heroism in that scene, only consequences, only grief. Sometimes, when you lose somebody that was special to you, you might see yourself in Cooper: watching life move forward without you. Watching people build something elsewhere, choose other people, choose other situations.

![Quote](/assets/img/reviews/interstellar-10.png)

It hurts to watch time create distance that cannot be undone. You can plan. You can promise. You can do everything in your power to change something. You can believe you will come back, that maybe they will wait, do something to have space for you in their lives. But you cannot pause the clock for the people you love, they also cannot pause the clock for you. Sometimes you have to leave to stop hurting other people. Sometimes you have to leave because you never really had a place you could call home in their lives. And sometimes, people just don't choose you. It is just life.

When Cooper detaches and falls into Gargantua, it is not triumph. It is surrender.

![Gargantua](/assets/img/reviews/interstellar-2.png)

Inside the tesseract, he realizes he was the ghost. He was always there, behind the bookshelf, trying to reach across time.

![Tesseract and the bookshelf](/assets/img/reviews/interstellar-4.png)

But when he hits the shelves, he is not powerful. He is desperate. He sees himself leaving. He sees her begging him to stay. And he is shouting as well, begging himself to stay. But he understands that it has already happened. He cannot undo it. He can only send a signal. He can encode data in a watch. He can knock. But no matter how hard he tries, he cannot go back.

![STAY](/assets/img/reviews/interstellar-16.png)

That is the part of Interstellar that hurts the most. Not the black hole. Not the physics. The realization that even if you could scream across dimensions, you still cannot rewrite what has already been written. There are moments in life that feel like that. Moments when you want to hit the walls of time and say try harder, stay longer, do something differently. But time does not open. People continue their lives, they don't change or they move forward. They build elsewhere. They drift further away. And you remain with the awareness of what could have been.Ultimately, humanity survives. Murph solves the equation. The mission worked. But Cooper does not get his life back. When he meets Murph again, she is elderly, and on her deathbed. Surrounded by her own family. The reunion is brief. She tells him to leave, no parent should watch their child die.

![Cooper and elderly Murph](/assets/img/reviews/interstellar-13.png)

Interstellar is not really about space. For many, it may be about love, but for me, it is about loss and grief. Time as something irreversible. Love is something that connects but does not protect you from consequence. And the painful understanding that sometimes life moves in only one direction. You can send signals. You can try to matter. You can hope the message lands. But you cannot retrieve what has already passed. Sometimes you are Cooper, left watching the recordings of a life that continues without you. And you cannot undo anything. Sometimes all you can do is accept that this is how it happened.

![Endurance heading back into space](/assets/img/reviews/interstellar-1.png)

title: Puella Magi Madoka Magica
desc: A person becomes naive if they're too kind. Careless if they're too bold. But the ultimate tragedy is when protection becomes a cage. In the end, only the Truth can break the cycle of witches.
body:
People love comparing Madoka to Christ. The final act, the cosmic scale, the idea of salvation through self-offering… there are real parallels. But there is someone else, working in the shadows of a self-imposed purgatory, who goes through constant pain and misery.

It's Homura.

Madoka and Homura together form a more complete messianic image than Madoka by herself. Not because you can add their virtues, but because the dynamic between them creates the shape of sacrifice. Their love isn’t just a feeling - it becomes a force that bends history, but it is also a force that can fracture it.

And for me, personally, there’s a second layer to all of this. I see myself in Madoka—the one who is constantly lured by the weight of compassion—and I recognize someone in my life as my “Homura.” They are the one whose devotion and silent suffering started to feel like a self-imposed destiny, a shield that eventually became a wall.

Homura’s mission is lonely. Most of her battles happen offscreen. She’s collecting grief seeds, patching cracks, and buying time. She is always there when Madoka is about to be pulled into something irreversible.

From Episode 4 onward, Homura makes one thing clear: Madoka doesn’t have to become a magical girl.

And that creates a temptation dynamic: Madoka is given the freedom to act and decide on her own.

![Kyubey tempting Madoka into making a wish](/assets/img/reviews/madoka-2.png)

Kyubey doesn’t tempt Madoka once. He tempts her repeatedly, in different costumes: duty, power, godhood. First, he sells her a “solution” (save your friends). Then he sells her significance (you could be great). Then he sells her transcendence (you could become more than human).

It echoes something very old: the temptation to solve the world through your own elevation. Something that deeply resonates with me. I see parts of me in Madoka—exploitable precisely because of a desire to help—while my Homura is the one who blocks the bait, acting as a guardian who keeps Madoka’s freedom intact just long enough for Madoka to choose **rightly**.

Timing matters. There’s a reason it would be wrong for Madoka to accept Kyubey’s deal on Kyubey’s terms. The whole story is about the difference between a coerced sacrifice and a chosen one.

![Madoka and Homura in many timelines](/assets/img/reviews/madoka-3.png)

If Madoka is the image of compassion, Homura is the image of endurance. I don’t know many fictional characters written with this level of relentless suffering. Homura suffers across timelines, watching the person she cares about die or collapse into despair. To keep going, she performs a spiritual amputation: the soft girl… moemura… becomes iron. She believes tenderness will fail the mission.

She accepts being misunderstood. She even accepts being hated, if that’s the price of keeping Madoka alive. This is where the story becomes quietly theological. A savior figure isn’t just someone who performs a glorious act; a savior is someone who **absorbs cost**. And Homura absorbs the cost of Madoka’s innocence.

The tragedy is that the more she sacrifices, the less anyone can understand her. The more she tries to act, the worse it gets. Homura tried to be strong enough to save Madoka, but it’s when she breaks that she is finally seen.

![Homura's bloody tear](/assets/img/reviews/madoka-4.png)

After that, Homura enters her loneliest stretch. This is where the Gethsemane parallel starts to shimmer. Jesus submits: “Not my will, but Yours.” 

Homura’s prayer is inverted, twisted. She doesn’t want her own cup removed; she wants to take the cup away from Madoka. But at some point, the person you love has to carry their own destiny. You can fight a hundred wars for them, but you cannot drink the cup that was never yours—especially if you yourself are not in a place to be solid ground for someone. You end up saving someone who is not grounded in your life in any physical sense, pulling them into a void they never asked for.

Homura reaches the point where her strategy collapses because she loses hope. Kyubey defeats her by narrating her suffering as meaningless. That’s how despair works: “None of this mattered. The chaos never ends.”

But then Madoka arrives. She uses the system against itself. She makes a wish that destroys the logic of witches at its root—choosing to carry the burden of the entire world’s hope. Kyubey confuses sacrifice with losing, but the Cross looks like defeat until it becomes the mechanism of victory. Through death, death is broken.

![Madoka's wish](/assets/img/reviews/madoka-5.png)

Madoka’s ascension remakes the universe. A new order appears: hope is no longer harvested as fuel for doom; it becomes part of a redeemed structure. But Madoka is nowhere to be seen. She is "everywhere and nowhere," having achieved a state of Resonance that the physical world can no longer contain.

![Homura and Madoka's mother sitting together](/assets/img/reviews/madoka-6.png)

If you isolate Madoka, she looks triumphant. If you isolate Homura, she looks tragic. But together, you see the full shape of sacrifice.

![Homura with Madoka's ribbon](/assets/img/reviews/madoka-7.png)

...it would be nice if it ended there. But things turn down the wrong path in *Rebellion*. Homura decides she wants to free Madoka from whatever 'illusion' of a life she thinks she lives, but it reveals a dark truth: **love without consent to transcendence easily turns into control.** 

It’s easy to watch Homura and think: “That’s love.” But protection can turn into a cage. Love can turn into obsession. When Homura refuses to let Madoka be what she truly is (God/Truth), she becomes the Demon (Akuma), trapping the one she loves in a false, edit-heavy mirage just to keep them near. We don’t really know what happens next. The last movie was delayed again, with no date in sight. It would be funny and ironic to see this one story unfinished as well—left in the silence between a forced cage and a chosen freedom.

![Rebellion](/assets/img/reviews/madoka-8.png)
